To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the use of multiple threshold voltage (V-T) devices in the same circuit can reduce standby leakage power by a factor of 10, and can reduce active leakage power by a similar factor, but requires a new process and design flow; 2) the use of a low V-T device in the same circuit as high V-T devices can reduce standby leakage by a factor of two, and active leakage by a factor that is a function of the fraction of the circuit that is implemented

the following circuit techniques are useful in reducing leakage power in deep-submicron designs: (1) use of a low threshold voltage for standby, and a high threshold voltage for active operation, (2) use of a high threshold voltage in standby, and a low threshold voltage in active operation, and (3) using a high threshold voltage and a low VDD in standby, and low threshold voltage and a high VDD in active operation.

the best approach to reducing leakage in a design is to reduce the supply voltage and use the standby mode to reduce the leakage.
the best approach for leakage power management is to design for a low leakage standby mode.
there is no single approach that is optimal for all designs, and that the choice of approach depends on a number of factors including technology, design style, application and cost.

a combination of design techniques is required to manage leakage power in deep-submicron CMOS.

a combination of design techniques, such as power gating, body biasing, and clock gating, is required to manage leakage in future designs.
